part1.text: Every enterprise has built this pilot. An AI that reads every policy in seconds… and acts on none of them.
So the employee closes the chat, logs into three portals, and does the work by hand. The human is still the copy-paste bus.
Enterprise AI moves through four stages. The real chasm is between an agent that acts with shared keys, and one that acts under governance.
The rule is simple. The model proposes. Deterministic services decide. The model never holds a credential, and never grades its own permissions.
Between a sentence and a system of record, there are nine gates: identity, policy, approval, a signed one-time grant, and a tamper-evident audit trail.
Same assistant, three requests. A leave request executes. A salary change is blocked by policy. A poisoned spreadsheet never gets a grant.
And friction scales with blast radius. Not every action needs a human. Some need two.
Part one of Governed Autonomy. Explore the interactive article at Ahmed Shaker dot com.

part2.text: Would you give your ERP keys to software that one sentence in a PDF can reprogram? No CISO would. Yet that's how most AI agents are wired.
Hide one instruction in row forty-two of a vendor spreadsheet, and a naive agent changes the bank details. No firewall was breached. It just read a poisoned row.
System prompts are advice, not security boundaries. That's authorization in client-side JavaScript.
And your API gateway approves four failures it can't see: prompt injection, the confused deputy, retry amplification, and tool drift.
So assume the model will be tricked, and contain it anyway, behind five trust boundaries.
Run the same poisoned file through a governed pipeline. It's filtered, delimited, and denied by policy. Zero execution grants. Nothing reaches the ERP.
Four rules before any agent gets write access: no ambient authority, no model-filled identity, no blind retries, and no dispatch without a signed grant.
Part two of Governed Autonomy. The full interactive article is at ahmed shaker dot com.

part3.text: Every department is building its own AI. Each with its own prompts, guardrails, and logs.
Five assistants, five guardrail schemes, five audit formats, and not one shared kill switch. It's the integration mess of the two-thousands, all over again.
Governance should never live inside the application. Capabilities should be governed contracts, not code.

Whether a system speaks OpenAPI, MCP, or a native SDK, it becomes one canonical contract, with a risk tier, hidden identity fields, and a pinned hash. The model plans against the contract, never the raw endpoint.
Nothing reaches production by default. A connector exposes a hundred and forty operations. All are quarantined. Only twelve make it through review and certification.
And when a tool changes overnight, its hash no longer matches. The new version is quarantined, while the live one keeps serving.
Govern once. Connect everything. One policy engine, one audit trail, one kill switch.
